questions.text: Classification models
questions.explanation: Classification models are supervised learning algorithms whose target variable is categorical (binary or multi-class), predicting which category a new observation belongs to. Common examples include logistic regression, decision trees, Random Forest, and XGBoost.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Classification & Regression/🎲 Classification models.md

options.text: A supervised learning algorithm family whose target variable is a category, predicting which class a new observation belongs to.
A supervised learning algorithm family whose target variable is a continuous number, predicting a numeric value for new observations.
An unsupervised technique that groups observations by feature similarity alone, with no predefined category labels to predict.
An unsupervised technique that finds 'if A then B' relationships between items that frequently co-occur within the same transaction.

questions.text: A model must predict which of five predefined categories a support ticket belongs to, using labeled historical tickets. Which type of supervised task is this?
questions.explanation: Classification models predict a categorical target variable; contrast with regression models, which predict a continuous number.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Classification & Regression/🎲 Classification models.md

questions.text: Decision trees
questions.explanation: A decision tree recursively splits data on feature thresholds to build a tree of decision rules, ending in leaf nodes that hold a class label or numeric value. A single unpruned tree has low bias but high variance, easily overfitting.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Classification & Regression/🎲 decision trees.md

options.text: A supervised algorithm that splits data on feature thresholds, ending in leaf nodes that hold a class label or numeric value.
A bagging ensemble of decision trees, each trained on a bootstrapped sample with a random subset of features considered per split.
A boosting ensemble of decision trees trained sequentially, where each new tree corrects the residual errors of the prior ensemble.
An algorithm that partitions observations into k groups by repeatedly assigning points to the nearest centroid and recomputing it.

questions.text: A lender needs to explain exactly why each loan application was approved or denied to a non-technical auditor, tracing the precise rule path behind every individual decision. Which model best satisfies this need for full transparency?
questions.explanation: A single decision tree is highly interpretable because you can trace the exact threshold-based rule path for any prediction, unlike ensembles that trade transparency for accuracy.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Classification & Regression/🎲 decision trees.md

options.text: Decision tree

questions.text: Logistic regression
questions.explanation: Logistic regression is a linear classification algorithm that models the probability of a binary outcome by applying a sigmoid function to a weighted linear combination of features. Despite its name it is a classifier, not a regressor.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Classification & Regression/🎲 logistic regression.md

options.text: A linear classification algorithm that models the probability of a binary outcome via a sigmoid over a weighted feature sum.
A SageMaker built-in algorithm that fits linear regression and classification models together in one unified, configurable algorithm.
An instance-based algorithm that predicts an observation's label from a majority vote among its k closest neighbors by distance.
A supervised algorithm that recursively splits data on feature thresholds, ending in leaf nodes that hold a predicted class.

questions.text: A team wants a fast-training binary classifier for a roughly linearly separable credit-approval dataset, where coefficients must clearly show each feature's direction of influence. Which algorithm fits best?
questions.explanation: Logistic regression models the probability of a binary outcome via a sigmoid over a linear combination of features, giving directly interpretable coefficients and fast training on simpler, linearly separable data.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Classification & Regression/🎲 logistic regression.md

options.text: Logistic regression

questions.text: Regression models
questions.explanation: Regression models are supervised learning algorithms whose target variable is a continuous numerical value, predicting that value for new observations. They are evaluated with metrics like RMSE or MAE, never classification metrics.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Classification & Regression/🎲 Regression models.md

options.text: A supervised learning algorithm family whose target variable is a continuous number, predicting a numeric value for new observations.
A supervised learning algorithm family whose target variable is a category, predicting which class or label an observation belongs to.
An unsupervised technique that groups observations purely by feature similarity, without a target value to predict at all.
An unsupervised technique that finds 'if A then B' relationships between items frequently co-occurring in the same transaction.

questions.text: A model must predict a house's sale price, a continuous numeric value, from historical sales data. Which type of supervised task is this?
questions.explanation: Regression models predict a continuous numerical target, in contrast to classification (categorical targets) or forecasting (sequential, time-ordered targets).
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Classification & Regression/🎲 Regression models.md

questions.text: Deep neural network (DNN)
questions.explanation: A DNN is a neural network with multiple hidden layers, allowing it to learn increasingly abstract feature representations at each successive layer. It requires substantially more data and compute than shallow models.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Deep Learning/🎲 deep neural network (DNN).md

options.text: A neural network with multiple stacked hidden layers, letting it learn increasingly abstract feature representations at each layer.
A general family of algorithms built from interconnected nodes with weighted sums and activations, without specifying how many layers.
A neural network architecture that maintains a hidden state across time steps, designed specifically for sequential data.
An optimization algorithm that iteratively adjusts a model's parameters in the direction that reduces a loss function.

questions.text: An image-classification model must learn its own hierarchical features directly from raw pixels, progressing from edges to shapes to objects, and requires GPU-scale training. Which approach fits?
questions.explanation: A deep neural network's many stacked hidden layers learn increasingly abstract, hierarchical feature representations from unstructured data, unlike tabular algorithms such as XGBoost.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Deep Learning/🎲 deep neural network (DNN).md

questions.text: Gradient descent (SGD)
questions.explanation: Gradient descent is the optimization algorithm used to train models by iteratively adjusting parameters to reduce a loss function's gradient. Stochastic Gradient Descent approximates that gradient using a small random batch at each step.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Deep Learning/🎲 gradient descent (SGD).md

options.text: An optimization algorithm that iteratively adjusts parameters to reduce loss; SGD approximates the gradient from a small random batch.
An ensemble technique that trains decision trees sequentially, each on a random subsample of rows and columns from the dataset.
A penalty added to a loss function proportional to the sum of squared weights, shrinking large weights toward zero.
A hyperparameter optimization strategy that samples random combinations of values instead of testing every combination exhaustively.

questions.text: A dataset is too large to compute the exact gradient over the full training set at every optimization step. Which technique makes iterative training tractable by approximating the gradient using small random batches?
questions.explanation: Stochastic Gradient Descent approximates the gradient using a small random batch each step, trading some update accuracy for much faster, more scalable training; it is a distinct concept from the similarly-named stochastic gradient boosting.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Deep Learning/🎲 gradient descent (SGD).md

questions.text: L2 regularization
questions.explanation: L2 regularization adds a penalty to a model's loss function proportional to the sum of squared weights, discouraging large weights and reducing overfitting. Unlike L1, it shrinks weights toward zero but rarely to exactly zero.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Deep Learning/🎲 L2 regularization.md

options.text: A penalty added to a loss function proportional to the sum of squared weights, shrinking large weights without zeroing them out.
A penalty added to a loss function proportional to the sum of absolute weights, capable of shrinking some weights exactly to zero.
An optimization algorithm that iteratively adjusts a model's parameters in the direction that reduces a loss function.
An ensemble technique that trains trees sequentially on random subsamples of rows and columns to reduce overfitting.

questions.text: A linear regression model has many correlated features and performs far better on training data than on validation data. Which fix shrinks all weights toward zero, but rarely to exactly zero, producing a smoother decision boundary?
questions.explanation: L2 regularization penalizes the sum of squared weights, shrinking large weights toward zero without zeroing them out, unlike L1 regularization, which can drive some weights exactly to zero for feature selection.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Deep Learning/🎲 L2 regularization.md

questions.text: Neural network
questions.explanation: A neural network is a layered algorithm of interconnected nodes, each applying a weighted sum plus a non-linear activation, that can learn complex, non-linear relationships. It is trained via gradient descent and backpropagation.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Deep Learning/🎲 Neural network.md

options.text: A layered network of interconnected nodes applying weighted sums and non-linear activations to learn complex relationships.

A neural network architecture that maintains a hidden state across time steps to model sequential, time-dependent data.
An optimization algorithm that iteratively adjusts a model's weights to minimize a loss function during training.

questions.text: A model needs to capture complex, non-linear relationships in raw audio waveforms, where traditional tabular algorithms don't apply well. Which approach is best suited?
questions.explanation: Neural networks learn complex, non-linear relationships from unstructured data like audio, images, or text, whereas algorithms like XGBoost usually win on structured tabular data instead.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Deep Learning/🎲 Neural network.md

questions.text: AdaBoost
questions.explanation: AdaBoost is a boosting algorithm that trains a sequence of weak learners, where each new learner focuses more on observations the previous learner misclassified by increasing their sample weight. It is not a SageMaker built-in algorithm.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Ensemble Algorithms/🎲 AdaBoost.md

options.text: A boosting algorithm that trains weak learners sequentially, increasing the weight of observations the previous learner misclassified.
A boosting technique that trains weak learners sequentially, each one fitted to the residual errors of the prior ensemble.
A bagging ensemble that trains decision trees independently and in parallel on bootstrapped samples of the data.
A boosting technique that trains trees sequentially on random subsamples of rows and columns each round, reducing variance.

questions.text: A boosting method trains a sequence of shallow decision trees, where each new tree increases the sample weight of observations the previous tree misclassified. Which algorithm is being described?
questions.explanation: AdaBoost re-weights misclassified observations after each round of weak learners, unlike gradient boosting, which instead fits new trees to the ensemble's residual errors.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Ensemble Algorithms/🎲 AdaBoost.md

questions.text: Gradient Boosting
questions.explanation: Gradient Boosting builds an ensemble of weak learners sequentially, where each new tree predicts the residual errors of the ensemble so far via gradient descent on a loss function. It generalizes to any differentiable loss.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Ensemble Algorithms/🎲 Gradient Boosting.md

options.text: A boosting technique that trains decision trees sequentially, each new tree fitted to the residual errors of the ensemble so far.

questions.text: A boosting ensemble must support both classification and regression by fitting each new tree to the residual errors of the ensemble so far via gradient descent on a differentiable loss, rather than reweighting misclassified samples. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: Gradient Boosting generalizes boosting to any differentiable loss function by fitting new trees to residual errors, unlike AdaBoost, which reweights misclassified samples and is framed mainly for classification.

questions.text: Random Forest
questions.explanation: Random Forest is a bagging ensemble of decision trees: each tree trains on a bootstrapped sample, and only a random subset of features is considered at each split. Trees are trained independently and in parallel, fixing high variance.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Ensemble Algorithms/🎲 Random Forest.md

questions.text: A single decision tree is badly overfitting a tabular customer-churn dataset. The team wants many decorrelated trees trained independently in parallel on bootstrapped samples, voting on the final prediction. Which technique fits?
questions.explanation: Random Forest bags decision trees on bootstrapped samples with random feature subsets at each split, training them independently and in parallel to reduce the variance that causes a single tree to overfit.

questions.text: Stochastic gradient boosting
questions.explanation: Stochastic Gradient Boosting extends Gradient Boosting by training each sequential tree on a random subsample of rows (and often columns) rather than the full dataset. This is the mechanism behind XGBoost's subsample hyperparameters.

questions.text: An XGBoost model is overfitting on training data. The team lowers `subsample` and `colsample_bytree` so each round of trees trains on a random subset of rows and columns instead of the full dataset. Which technique are they applying?
questions.explanation: Stochastic gradient boosting extends gradient boosting with row/column subsampling per tree, adding regularization that reduces overfitting; this is exactly the mechanism behind XGBoost's subsample and colsample_bytree hyperparameters.

questions.explanation: Association rule learning is an unsupervised technique that discovers 'if A, then B' relationships between items that frequently co-occur together in transactions, most commonly associated with market basket analysis. Rules are evaluated using support, confidence, and lift.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Unsupervised learning/🎲 Association rule learning.md

questions.explanation: Association rule learning discovers if-A-then-B relationships between items that frequently co-occur in the same transaction, evaluated with support, confidence, and lift.

questions.text: Clustering
questions.explanation: Clustering is an unsupervised task that groups observations into clusters based purely on similarity of their features, with no predefined labels. Its quality is judged with internal metrics or domain review, not accuracy/F1.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Unsupervised learning/🎲 Clustering.md

questions.text: K-Means Clustering
questions.explanation: K-Means is a clustering algorithm that partitions observations into k clusters by iteratively assigning each point to its nearest centroid and recalculating centroids until assignments stabilize. It requires choosing k in advance and prior feature scaling.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Unsupervised learning/🎲 K-Means Clustering.md

An unsupervised task that groups observations by feature similarity, without specifying how the groups are formed.

questions.text: Random Cut Forest (RCF)
questions.explanation: Random Cut Forest is a SageMaker built-in unsupervised algorithm for anomaly detection: it builds an ensemble of trees by randomly partitioning the data and scores each observation by how easily it is isolated. It natively supports streaming data.
questions.source: Machine Learning Algorithms/Unsupervised learning/🎲 Random Cut Forest (RCF).md

questions.text: A team must detect unusual spikes in IoT sensor readings streamed in near real time, with no pre-existing labeled dataset of anomalous events to train a supervised classifier on. Which SageMaker built-in algorithm fits, pairing naturally with a Kinesis stream?
questions.explanation: Random Cut Forest is an unsupervised anomaly-detection algorithm that scores how anomalous each observation is via a tree ensemble, and natively supports streaming data.
